content:
Quick answer

Living with arthritis can affect far more than a painful joint. Getting dressed, working, sleeping and keeping plans may take more effort. The right support depends on the type of arthritis you have and what matters to you. Treatment, suitable exercise, practical changes and support with your feelings can all have a place. You do not have to work it out alone.

When ordinary things take more effort

A stiff morning can change the rest of your day. You might need longer to get ready, find a familiar task harder or wonder whether you have enough energy for plans later on. Other people may not see that extra effort.

Arthritis affects people differently. Symptoms can include joint pain, stiffness, swelling and reduced movement. Some forms of arthritis can also cause fatigue and affect other parts of the body. A diagnosis helps your healthcare team explain what is happening and choose suitable treatment. This article is about everyday life, not a way to diagnose yourself.

Start with the part of life that is hardest at the moment. That might be getting out of a chair, doing your job, sleeping comfortably or keeping up with family. A specific example gives your healthcare team something useful to work on with you.

A more manageable day

Give yourself room in the morning

If stiffness makes mornings difficult, allow more time where you can. Keep the things you need within easy reach and follow the movement plan agreed with your healthcare professional. New, prolonged or worsening stiffness deserves a review rather than being dismissed as part of getting older.

Adapt a task before giving it up

Changing how you do something is different from giving up on it. An occupational therapist can help with everyday activities, protecting your joints and equipment or changes that make tasks easier. For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE recommends access to occupational therapy when daily activities or hand function are difficult.

Choose one task to discuss: opening containers, dressing, cooking, using a keyboard or getting in and out of a chair. Explain what happens, how often it happens and what help you already use.

Find a balance between activity and rest

With rheumatoid arthritis, NHS advice is to find a balance between rest and exercise and build activity up gradually. Long periods without movement can leave joints stiffer and muscles weaker. During a flare, you may need more rest and advice about adapting your usual activity.

Pacing is about finding an amount you can manage, rather than doing everything on a better day and being left exhausted. Your physiotherapist or occupational therapist can help you plan this around your condition and responsibilities.

Movement should fit you

There is no single exercise plan for everyone with arthritis. Your condition, symptoms, other health problems and confidence all matter.

For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends exercise tailored to your needs, including muscle strengthening and aerobic fitness. Pain can increase when you first start. That does not mean you should expect every exercise to feel easy, but it also does not mean you should push through any symptom. Ask for help with the type, amount and progression of exercise if you are unsure.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE recommends access to specialist physiotherapy, including help with fitness, flexibility and strength. A warm, swollen joint or severe pain during an activity needs a different response from ordinary effort. Stop that activity and seek advice if symptoms are new, severe or not settling. A sudden hot, swollen or very painful joint needs urgent assessment, as explained below.

Our arthritis exercise hub can help you find information to discuss with your healthcare team. It is not a personalised exercise prescription.

Keep treatment questions on the agenda

Take prescribed medicines as directed. If you are worried about side effects, do not simply struggle on or change the dose yourself. Speak to your prescriber, pharmacist or rheumatology team. Check before adding an over-the-counter painkiller or supplement, because it may interact with your treatment.

If you have inflammatory arthritis, feeling better does not necessarily mean you no longer need treatment. Ask your team before reducing or stopping a medicine.

It can help to keep a short note of what has changed: symptoms, sleep, activities you cannot manage, medicine concerns and questions. Take that note to your next appointment.

Work, money and asking for help

Arthritis can make work or caring responsibilities harder. Tell your healthcare team which tasks are affected. Occupational therapy may help you think through practical changes.

If work or money is a concern, use our Benefits and PIP hub as a starting point for further information. A diagnosis alone does not decide entitlement, and this article does not assess eligibility.

At home, a specific request may be easier for someone else to act on than a general request for help. For example: "Could you carry the shopping today?" or "I would like to come, but I may need to leave earlier." These are conversation ideas, not medical instructions.

Your feelings count too

Pain, fatigue and uncertainty can affect how you feel. Frustration, worry or changes in confidence deserve attention as well as joint symptoms.

NHS advice for rheumatoid arthritis is to speak to your healthcare team if you are struggling with your feelings. Talking to someone with a similar condition may also help. Support is not a sign that you have failed to cope.

Tell a GP or another healthcare professional if low mood or anxiety is persistent or affecting daily life. Pain and tiredness should not have to become unbearable before you ask for help.

When to seek medical help

See a GP for unexplained joint pain, stiffness or swelling that does not settle in a few days. Arrange a review for new or worsening fatigue or increasing difficulty with daily activities.

Persistent joint swelling may need specialist assessment. NICE says suspected persistent synovitis of unknown cause should be referred for specialist opinion. Referral should be urgent when the small joints of the hands or feet or more than one joint are affected, or when there has been a delay of three months or longer before seeking advice. Normal blood tests or negative rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP tests do not rule out the need for urgent referral. Tests should not delay it. A clinician must assess whether this applies to you.

A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent assessment, even without a fever. Do not assume it is an ordinary flare or gout attack. In England, Scotland and Wales, ask for an urgent GP appointment or call 111. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service.

Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency. Confusion, severe breathing difficulty or blue, pale or blotchy skin during a possible infection need emergency help. NHS sepsis advice explains these warning signs.

One useful next step

You do not need to change your whole routine today. Choose one difficulty and one question to take to your healthcare team.

  • "Getting dressed is taking much longer. Could occupational therapy help?"
  • "I want to move more, but I am not sure what amount is right for me."
  • "My symptoms have changed. Does my treatment need reviewing?"
  • "Pain and tiredness are affecting how I feel. What support is available?"

The aim is a plan that supports your life, with room to change it when your needs change.

Frequently asked questions

Can people live well with arthritis?

Many people continue activities that matter to them with treatment and suitable support. What that looks like is individual. Osteoarthritis does not necessarily keep getting worse, and inflammatory arthritis needs appropriate treatment and monitoring.

Should I rest or exercise?

Both can have a place. Suitable exercise is part of osteoarthritis care, and rheumatoid arthritis care includes support to balance activity and rest. Ask for advice that fits your condition, especially during a flare. A sudden hot, swollen or very painful joint needs urgent assessment rather than an exercise adjustment.

Who can help with everyday tasks?

Your GP or rheumatology team can advise about available support. Occupational therapists can help with daily activities and hand function; physiotherapists can help with movement, fitness and exercise. Access depends on your needs and local services.

Can arthritis affect mood and relationships?

Pain, fatigue and changes in confidence can affect mood and closeness with other people. Talk to your healthcare team if you are struggling. You can also explain to family or friends what would make a particular activity easier.
